notes:
One sentence in one finding, which had been guessing at a cause for every site that saw it.

When Docket found more structured-data blocks of a type than there were pages, it explained the difference the same way every time: "a listing or variant picker repeats the type, and each copy is read separately." The count beside that clause is measured against the markup and is right. The clause itself was written from a guess about how a shop is built, and it was attached to every site regardless.

On a large publisher's blog it was wrong. 100 Organization blocks across 50 pages, and not one of them is a listing — they are `@id` references, two per page, pointing at a definition the page never provides. A reader sent looking for a variant picker would not find one, and the fix is the opposite shape: define the node once, rather than de-duplicate copies.

Docket already resolves `@id` references a step earlier, so it can tell the two apart. The sentence is now computed from the same data the count came from, and says which it is: every block a reference to a missing definition — naming the id, so you can search for it — or some of them references and the rest genuine repeats, or a real listing, which still reads exactly as it did.

Nothing else changed. A re-audit of the same site on this build gained no findings and lost none; only that sentence is different.
